claims.text: Conventional consolidation can produce a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
The proposed intervention is to deposit a uniform approximately 100 nm Mo coating on W surfaces by PVD before composite consolidation.
The proposed process includes a post-sintering anneal at 800–850 °C in an inert atmosphere.
Pre-coating W with approximately 100 nm of Mo will create a continuous, thin Mo interlayer at W/Cu interfaces after consolidation and annealing.
Mo has good chemical compatibility with both W and Cu.
A Mo interlayer at a W/Cu interface acts as a diffusion barrier.
A Mo interlayer improves wetting and bonding between W and Cu.
Improved interfacial wetting and diffusion-barrier behavior suppress diffusion-driven phase separation and void nucleation during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically suffer interfacial phase separation and void formation under thermal and irradiation stresses.
Interfacial phase separation and void formation degrade the thermal conductivity and overall joint performance of untreated W–Cu composites.
Mo-coated W–Cu composites will retain better interfacial integrity and form fewer voids than untreated W–Cu composites under matched service conditions.
Reduced interfacial damage in the Mo-coated composite will result in higher thermal conductivity than in an untreated W–Cu composite.
The intervention is expected to be effective for conventionally consolidated W-particle or W-ligament/Cu-matrix composites annealed at 800–850 °C.
The intervention is expected to remain effective under high heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to W-based plasma-facing material/Cu-based cooling-component joints.
Uniform PVD coating of complex W-ligament topologies may be difficult.
The long-term stability of the Mo interlayer under prolonged irradiation is uncertain.
